newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Caspian oil transit deal seen as only a first step.
newsitem.headline: Caspian oil transit deal seen as only a first step.

text.p: A hard-won agreement between Russia, Azerbaijan and Chechnya at the weekend to transport Caspian crude to world markets will not be the last word on the thorny issue of who will control the world's newest oil.
"It's a complicated bunch of interests," said Sergei Markov of the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace in Moscow.

First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, also energy minister, signed the long-delayed deal to export Caspian oil via a Russian pipeline late on Friday, affording a sigh of relief to a 13-member international oil consortium which will use the link later this year.
A second breakthrough came on Saturday when Russia's Fuel and Energy Ministry and the Chechen oil company YUNKO signed their own deal to get the link into a working state on time.

Under the deals, Chechnya agreed to cooperate in the transport of oil through the 1,500-km link, 160 km of which run through the separatist Russian region and which connects the Azeri capital Baku to Russia's Novorossiisk on the Black Sea.

Chechnya, which fought a bloody 21-month battle against Russian forces, ending in humiliation for Moscow when Russian troops withdrew last year, had said previous agreements were not valid and demanded a cut in transport tariffs.

Analysts familiar with the geopolitics of exporting oil from a region whose supplies could rival those of the Middle East say the deals are not the last word -- especially since the pipeline tariff issue has not been resolved.
"This will not be the last agreement," said energy analyst Alexei Kokin of Renaissance Capital. "The pipeline could be a tool the Chechens use in case of disagreements with Moscow."
The deals involve many entities, all vying to influence the flow of energy from one of the world's last great oil provinces.

The party most immediately interested is the Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), the British Petroleum/Statoil-led group which plans to use the link several months after it begins producing oil at its three fields in the Caspian's Azeri sector in August.
"We are not yet familiar with the contents of the document (the agreement) and we can't comment on the provisions of the document," said AIOC president Terry Adams.
"But we are very much pleased that the document has been signed between Chechnya and Russia and SOCAR and now we are convinced that the northern pipeline will work."

Caspian oil reserves, which at a possible 100 billion barrels could be as great of those of Kuwait and triple those of the North Sea, have prompted a new "Great Game" on the eve of the 21st century, with the players this time foreign oil companies.
Tsars and British colonialists played out the original "Great Game" last century as they fought for influence in the region to shore up the boundaries of the Russian and Indian empires.
Britain has dropped out of the new version but post-Soviet Russia is keen to control the flow of oil from the region.
Complicating matters on Monday was Turkmenistan, which threatened to tighten controls over areas of the Caspian Sea, including AIOC's fields, which it claims are its territory.
Even top Russian officials said thorny issues remained.
"With the signing of these documents, the main step was completed, but there are still many steps ahead," Boris Berezovsky, chief Kremlin negotiator on the deal, told Interfax.
Chechen officials also spoke of the weekend agreements as not just about the economics of transporting oil.

"The document has not just economic but also great political significance for the republic," Interfax quoted YUNKO president Khodzhakhmed Yarikhanov as saying, arguing that it gave Chechnya recognition as a political entity.
He said 150 men, or about one for each km of the pipeline running through Chechnya, were available to guard the link.
"It is not out of the question that the pipeline territory will be declared off limits and that firearms may be used against anyone who violates that," Yarikhanov said.
